The Python proof showed the [PAVED](/blog/building-a-platform) layers without a cluster. [Kubernetes as a control plane](/blog/kubernetes-is-a-control-plane) is one substrate. Most teams already pay for another: AWS.

This is the same capability, same contract, different roadbed. DynamoDB instead of etcd. IAM Identity Center instead of an allowlist in a file. Step Functions instead of a for-loop. App Runner and Amplify instead of a compose file. Secrets Manager instead of a JSON blob on disk.

I wasn't trying to replace EKS. I wanted to know if the layers still hold when the data plane is real AWS services and there is no cluster to hide behind. They do. The tools change. The sequencing doesn't.

Each section is the local Python that implements a layer, then the one AWS service I'd actually use instead of keeping the Python. The shopping list is already in the PAVED post. This is the afternoon proving you can pave the road with managed services.

The code is at [github.com/richpeaua/platform-on-aws](https://github.com/richpeaua/platform-on-aws):

```bash
git clone https://github.com/richpeaua/platform-on-aws.git
cd platform-on-aws
python -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -e ".[dev]"
```

## The request

Same outcome as [from-scratch](/blog/platform-from-scratch). One field changed: `workload` instead of a bare `image`, because AWS has two compute answers and pretending otherwise leaks the infrastructure into the contract.

Container:

```yaml
apiVersion: platform/v1
kind: AppEnvironment
metadata:
  name: checkout
spec:
  team: payments
  tier: production
  domain: checkout.acme.io
  workload:
    type: container
    image: 123456789012.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/checkout:1.4.2
  components:
    database: postgres
    cache: true
  observability: true
```

Website:

```yaml
apiVersion: platform/v1
kind: AppEnvironment
metadata:
  name: checkout
spec:
  team: payments
  tier: production
  domain: checkout.acme.io
  workload:
    type: website
    repository: https://github.com/acme/checkout-web
    branch: main
    framework: nextjs
  components:
    database: postgres
```

No instance class. No VPC id. No Postgres version. `database: postgres` is the whole ask. `workload.type` is the only fork the developer is allowed to see: running container, or Git-backed site. App Runner vs Amplify is a fulfillment detail.

```bash
export PLATFORM_SSO_TEAM=payments
platform apply -f examples/checkout-container.yaml
platform get appenvironment checkout
```

```yaml
status:
  phase: Ready
  workloadType: container
  url: https://checkout.acme.io
  appRunnerServiceArn: arn:aws:apprunner:us-east-1:123456789012:service/checkout/...
  db_secret_ref: arn:aws:secretsmanager:us-east-1:123456789012:secret:environments/checkout/database/credentials
```

The password is not in that YAML. That's the point.

Build order is 0, then P, then V, then E, then A, then D. You expose the reverse. I'm not going to re-argue it.

## Layer 0: something has to store state

Same four things as the Python store: desired state, one write door, a way for fulfillment to notice, spec vs status. Skip this and every Lambda invents its own table. That's how you get six platforms that all talk to RDS.

Kubernetes bundles this as etcd plus the API server. AWS already sells the pieces:

| Need | AWS |
|---|---|
| Desired state | DynamoDB item, `pk=APENV#checkout`, `sk=META` |
| Write door | API Gateway → Lambda `apply()` |
| Watch | DynamoDB Streams → EventBridge |
| Observed state | status-only updates, conditional writes |

Locally I kept the DynamoDB shape and wrote JSON files:

```
data/dynamodb/APENV#checkout.json
```

```python
@dataclass
class Item:
    name: str
    spec: dict
    status: dict = field(default_factory=dict)
    principal_arn: str | None = None

    def to_dict(self) -> dict:
        return {
            "pk": f"APENV#{self.name}",
            "sk": "META",
            "name": self.name,
            "spec": self.spec,
            "status": self.status,
            "principal_arn": self.principal_arn,
        }
```

`apply` writes spec first, `phase: Pending`. Fulfillment writes status later. Humans don't get a field for `phase: Ready`.

```python
def apply(self, resource_dict: dict) -> Item:
    admitted = admit(resource_dict, self.principal)
    item = Item(
        name=admitted["metadata"]["name"],
        spec=admitted["spec"],
        status={"phase": "Pending"},
        principal_arn=self.principal.role_arn,
    )
    self.store.put(item)
    item = self.fulfill.run(item)
    self.store.put(item)
    return item
```

**Production: DynamoDB + Streams + EventBridge.** Don't rebuild a watch bus. The table in `infra/main.tf` is the whole substrate: pay-per-request, streams on, two keys. API Gateway is the hub. Every mutation goes through it: human apply, status write, catalog register. One door.

EKS is a valid Layer 0 on AWS. Using it here would collapse this post into the Kubernetes one. The interesting claim is that you can do this without operating a cluster.

## Layer P: a contract that doesn't leak how

Federation only works if teams integrate against a schema, not each other's Terraform. Three properties, none of them optional:

- The request states the outcome (`tier: production`), not the procedure (`aws apprunner create-service`).
- Bad requests die at submission, not in a Step Function at 2am.
- The producer can swap App Runner for Fargate. Consumers don't notice.

The public contract is JSON Schema, the same file API Gateway would validate:

```json
"workload": {
  "oneOf": [
    {
      "required": ["type", "image"],
      "properties": {
        "type": { "const": "container" },
        "image": { "type": "string" }
      }
    },
    {
      "required": ["type", "repository", "branch"],
      "properties": {
        "type": { "const": "website" },
        "repository": { "type": "string" },
        "branch": { "type": "string" }
      }
    }
  ]
}
```

What's missing is the whole argument. No `Cpu: 1 vCPU`. No `DBInstanceClass`. No GitHub PAT. Those live in nested stacks the developer never writes.

`platform explain appenvironment` dumps the schema. Apply `tier: prod` and it never reaches fulfillment:

```bash
platform apply -f bad-tier.yaml
# schema validation failed at spec.tier: 'prod' is not one of ...
```

**Production: API Gateway request validation.** Same JSON Schema, attached to the route. OpenAPI if you want generated clients. Proton template inputs and Service Catalog product parameters are the productized version of this layer. They are still a schema over an outcome. They are not a substitute for having one.

## Layer V: make the ask real, then keep it real

A contract with no fulfillment is a validated notebook. This layer binds it to the world.

On Kubernetes that's a controller loop. On AWS the closest managed shape is a state machine that you re-run when spec changes, not a one-shot Terraform apply from a laptop. Level-triggered: EventBridge sees the DynamoDB write, Step Functions runs, stacks converge, status goes back to the item.

The local Python is the same states as `infra/stepfunctions/app-environment.asl.json`:

```
ValidateSpec
  → BranchOnWorkloadType
       ├─ container → App Runner
       └─ website   → Amplify (CodeStar Connection)
  → RDS, if database: postgres
  → Secrets Manager
  → Route 53 + ACM
  → status Ready
  → catalog
```

```python
if workload["type"] == "container":
    status["appRunnerServiceArn"] = arn
elif workload["type"] == "website":
    status["amplifyAppId"] = app_id
    status["amplifyBranch"] = workload["branch"]
```

Two compute products, one capability. The contract didn't grow a second kind.

Secrets Manager is not an afterthought. RDS-managed master passwords (`ManageMasterUserPassword: true` in the CloudFormation) land in a secret. App Runner receives the ARN as a runtime environment secret, not a plaintext env var. Amplify gets the same ARN as `DATABASE_SECRET_ARN`. The spec has no `password` field. Admission rejects one if you try.

```python
def mint_database(self, name: str, host: str, *, owner: str) -> str:
    arn = secret_arn(name)
    self.put(arn, {
        "username": name,
        "password": secrets.token_urlsafe(24),
        "host": host,
        "port": 5432,
        "dbname": name,
    }, tags={"platform.corp/owner": owner})
    return arn
```

Locally that's a file under `data/secrets/`. In AWS that's an ARN on the status object:

```yaml
db_secret_ref: arn:aws:secretsmanager:us-east-1:123456789012:secret:environments/checkout/database/credentials
```

Git access for Amplify is a CodeStar Connection, not a PAT stuffed into a secret. Long-lived tokens are how websites bypass the platform. The connection is org-scoped, SSO-aligned, and the Amplify stack is only allowed `codestar-connections:UseConnection` on that ARN.

**Production: Step Functions + nested CloudFormation.** The ASL is in the repo. App Runner stack for containers:

```yaml
Service:
  Type: AWS::AppRunner::Service
  Properties:
    SourceConfiguration:
      ImageRepository:
        ImageIdentifier: !Ref Image
        ImageRepositoryType: ECR
        ImageConfiguration:
          RuntimeEnvironmentSecrets:
            - Name: DATABASE_URL
              Value: !Ref DatabaseSecretArn
```

Amplify stack for websites, Git via the connection, no `OauthToken`:

```yaml
App:
  Type: AWS::Amplify::App
  Properties:
    Repository: !Ref Repository
    IAMServiceRole: !GetAtt AmplifyRole.Arn
```

RDS with Secrets Manager owning the password:

```yaml
Instance:
  Type: AWS::RDS::DBInstance
  Properties:
    Engine: postgres
    MasterUsername: app
    ManageMasterUserPassword: true
```

Proton is the buy-vs-build shortcut at this layer. I'd name it, then still keep the contract and the branch on `workload.type`. The state machine is teaching the sequencing. Proton is what you point at once the sequencing is obvious.

`cache: true` is in the contract and not in the stacks. ElastiCache is a stretch. A field you don't fulfill yet is better than a second capability.

## Layer E: rails before on-ramps

Self-service without identity is a portal over a ticket queue. The from-scratch proof used a team allowlist. That's a toy. AWS already has the real thing: IAM Identity Center (SSO) and IAM.

Admission runs on every write, before DynamoDB. Secrets-in-spec first (clearest error), then schema, then IAM, then the rest. Fail before persist.

The caller is a principal, not a string in a YAML file:

```python
@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Principal:
    team: str
    role_arn: str
    role: str = "developer"
    allowed_workload_types: tuple[str, ...] = ("container", "website")

    @property
    def tags(self) -> dict[str, str]:
        return {"team": self.team}
```

Production: `aws sso login`, assume `PlatformDeveloper-payments`, session tag `team=payments`. API Gateway IAM auth. The Lambda reads the tag. Locally `PLATFORM_SSO_TEAM=payments` stands in for that session.

Four rules on top of schema:

```python
def validate_iam_team(resource, principal):
    if resource["spec"]["team"] != principal.tags["team"]:
        raise AdmissionError("IAM ABAC denied: ...")

def validate_domain_ownership(resource, principal):
    if domain not in TEAM_ALLOWED_DOMAINS[principal.team]:
        raise AdmissionError(f"domain '{domain}' is not owned by team '{principal.team}'")

def validate_production_no_latest(resource):
    if spec["tier"] == "production" and image_tag == "latest":
        raise AdmissionError("production requires a pinned image tag")

def validate_no_secrets_in_spec(resource):
    # password, token, api_key, ...
    raise AdmissionError("secret value must not appear in spec; use Secrets Manager")
```

A contractor role can drop `container` from `allowed_workload_types`. They can ship a website. They cannot ask for App Runner. That's IAM, not a comment in a runbook.

Break them. `--team identity` against a payments manifest dies at ABAC. `platform.acme.io` from payments dies at domain ownership. `checkout:latest` on production dies at the pin. `spec.password: hunter2` dies before schema even runs. None of them start a state machine.

**Production: IAM Identity Center + ABAC + a permission boundary.** The developer role is tagged `team=payments`. The API policy is "invoke only if that tag is present." The boundary denies IAM escalation and scopes Secrets Manager reads to `environments/${aws:PrincipalTag/team}/*`. SCPs at the org are the hard rails you don't put in Lambda: no public RDS, encryption required, no `platform:*` outside the platform account.

```json
{
  "Sid": "DenyUntaggedSessions",
  "Effect": "Deny",
  "Action": ["execute-api:Invoke"],
  "Resource": "arn:aws:execute-api:us-east-1:123456789012:platform/*",
  "Condition": {
    "Null": {
      "aws:PrincipalTag/team": "true"
    }
  }
}
```

IAM can require that you *have* a team tag. The Lambda still has to check that the tag matches `spec.team`. ABAC gets you to the door. Admission still reads the body.

The property that matters is *where* this runs: at the API, once, for every on-ramp. Not in each team's GitHub Action.

## Layer A: more than one door, same road

The contract is *what*. This layer is *how*. CLI, Service Catalog, an internal portal - all of them submit the same object and hit the same IAM + Lambda. A second path that clicks around in the Amplify console is a second platform you will forget to secure.

The Python has a CLI. Apply is thin on purpose. It carries the principal. It does not talk to DynamoDB.

```python
@cli.command()
def apply(ctx, files):
    platform = ctx.obj["platform"]
    for path in files:
        data = yaml.safe_load(path.read_text())
        resource = platform.apply(data)
        click.echo(f"{data['kind']}/{resource.name} applied")
```

```bash
aws sso login --profile platform-dev   # production
export PLATFORM_SSO_TEAM=payments      # local stand-in
platform apply -f examples/checkout-container.yaml
platform get appenvironment checkout
platform apply -f examples/checkout-website.yaml
```

**Production: SigV4 to API Gateway.** Same YAML, signed as the SSO role. Then the other doors: Service Catalog that assumes the same role, a Backstage template that POSTs the same body, Proton if that's what the org already bought. Three interfaces, one schema, one IAM policy, one state machine.

The failure mode is the "just for now" Amplify app created in the console with a PAT. Guardrails skipped. Catalog empty. That's not self-service. That's shadow IT with a nicer logo.

## Layer D: if they can't find it, it doesn't exist

Last because there's nothing to catalog until something is built, guarded, and reachable.

Two lists. Capabilities: the menu. Instances: things that actually got provisioned. Fulfillment registers an instance when status hits Ready. No extra sync job.

```python
self.catalog.register_instance(
    Instance(
        capability="app-environment",
        name=name,
        url=status["url"],
        owner=owner,
        workload_type=workload["type"],
    )
)
```

```bash
platform catalog list
# app-environment   Application Environment   owner=team-platform
# app-environment/checkout   container   https://checkout.acme.io   owner=payments

platform catalog search "environment"
```

Every provisioned resource is tagged the same way: `platform.corp/capability`, `platform.corp/owner`, `platform.corp/workload`. Secrets Manager secrets too. Cost, audit, and the catalog all follow the same keys.

Owner is the field people skip. A catalog without owners is a directory of tickets.

**Production: tags + a catalog index, then Backstage (or Port) if you need a UI.** AWS Service Catalog and Proton already list products. They don't replace an owner on every instance. When an environment goes Ready, register it and hang CloudWatch and the App Runner URL off it.

## One request, three stacks

Python from scratch:

```
CLI reads YAML
  → admission: schema, team, domain, :latest
  → hub writes spec
  → controllers emit children
  → JSON credentials on disk
  → status Ready
  → catalog
```

Kubernetes:

```
kubectl / Backstage
  → Kyverno + CRD schema
  → etcd
  → Kubebuilder
      App Runner analog: Deployment + Ingress
      website analog: you probably still want Amplify or a CDN
      PostgreSQL claim → Crossplane
      ExternalSecret ← Vault
  → .status
  → Backstage
```

AWS:

```
aws sso login + CLI
  → API Gateway IAM + JSON Schema
  → Lambda admission: team tag, domain, :latest, secrets-in-spec
  → DynamoDB
  → Step Functions
       container → App Runner
       website   → Amplify (CodeStar)
       RDS + Secrets Manager
  → .status
  → catalog + tags
```

Same sequence. Different machinery.

If I threw the Python away tomorrow, I'd keep the contract, the workload.type fork, IAM-before-CLI, secrets-never-in-spec, and catalog-last. I'd swap the JSON files for DynamoDB, the Pydantic models for API Gateway schema, the for-loop for Step Functions, the policy functions for IAM plus one Lambda, the `--team` flag for `aws sso login`, the dict-in-a-file catalog for tagged resources plus Backstage.

## What's fake

The control plane is real enough to feel: spec/status, SSO-shaped identity, admission order, fulfill branching, secret refs instead of values, catalog on Ready, tests for the happy path and the policy rejects.

The data plane is not. No live App Runner, Amplify, or RDS. `infra/` is the mapping you would deploy. I ran pytest, applied both examples by hand, and caught the secrets-in-spec rule getting shadowed by JSON Schema until the walk ran first. That's the verification. Not a well-architected review, not STS federation, not CI.

Team → domain ownership is a dict, not Identity Center group membership synced from the IdP. Observability is a CloudWatch dashboard name. ElastiCache is a field with no stack. Rotation exists as a sentence, not a lambda.

That's enough to feel why the layers exist on AWS. It is not enough to run a company on.

I already knew the services. Building the dumb version is what made the sequencing make sense.
